Wednesday, May 22, 2024, at 6:00 p.m.

Notice is hereby given that the Bluffdale City Council and Local Building Authority will hold a combined meeting on
Wednesday, May 22, 2024, at Bluffdale City Hall, 2222 West 14400 South, Bluffdale, Utah. The meeting will begin at 6:00 PM
or as soon thereafter as possible. This meeting will also be broadcast live to the public at: www.bluffdale.gov. The public
may comment at the meeting or by emailing comments to councilmeetingcomment@bluffdale.gov by 4:00 PM the day of
the meeting. Emailed comments will be submitted to the City Council but will not be read at the meeting. Notice is further
given that access to this meeting by the City Council may be by electronic means.
In the event the meeting is disrupted in any way that the City in its sole discretion deems inappropriate, the City reserves the
right to immediately remove the individual(s) from the meeting and, if needed, end virtual access to the meeting. Reasons
for removing an individual or ending virtual access to the meeting include but are not limited to the posting of offensive
pictures, remarks, or making offensive statements, disrespectful statements or actions, and any other action deemed
inappropriate.

31            2.1    Presentation and Discussion of Tentative Budget for the 2024-2025 Fiscal Year.
32                   (Staff Presenters, Stephanie Thayer and Bruce Kartchner).
33
34   Administrative Services Director, Bruce Kartchner, provided an overview of the Budget process. He
35   explained that the City is required by State law to pass a balanced Tentative Budget by the first
36   Tuesday in May. Bluffdale usually passes its Tentative Budget between late March and late April.
37   In 2024, they added a Budget Review Committee ("BRC"), which delayed the process slightly. Prior
38   to tentative approval, it is viewed as the City Manager's Budget. Once it passes, it is then the City
39   Council's Budget. After approval, the Council will continue with an in-depth review and discussions
40   and provide additional direction on the final numbers.


                                                      1
                            DRAFT – FOR DISCUSSION PURPOSES ONLY

                 BLUFFDALE CITY COUNCIL, LOCAL BUILDING AUTHORITY,
                 AND REDEVELOPMENT AGENCY BOARD MEETING MINUTES
                                Wednesday, April 24, 2024

 1
 2   There will be a Public Hearing at the City Council Meeting later that evening before the Tentative
 3   Budget is passed. The Final Budget must be passed at a Public Hearing in June. The Budget is what
 4   Staff anticipates will happen, but adjustments need to be made at various times, and amended Budgets
 5   will be presented throughout the year. That is a normal part of the process. As part of this process,
 6   the City Council will have the option to do a property tax increase, which will trigger a Truth in
 7   Taxation Hearing, a standalone hearing about proposed changes to property taxes in August.
 8
 9   The City Council had one meeting regarding the general Budget requirements where they heard from
10   all Departments about their needs, expectations, and desires. As part of that, Mr. Kartchner presented
11   an overview of budgeting concepts. He gave that overview again to help residents understand the
12   process.
13
14   When creating the Budget, Staff and the City Council identify what is important to residents and
15   business owners in the community. The government is set up to service residents and business
16   owners, so it needs to know what they want. As an example, a study was done with respect to what
17   is important to citizens. Parks and trails were identified as the highest and most important concern.
18   That is an important budgetary consideration.         Bluffdale is a very diverse city, and not just
19   geographically. It has wealthy, middle-class, and lower-income residents. It has empty nesters, young
20   families, and families with teens, as well as some families with all three. Some citizens are very
21   social, and others are more private. There is a variety of people in Bluffdale, and they all have
22   different priorities. It is up to the Staff and City Council to try to balance the different needs and
23   wants of citizens. That can be challenging due to money constraints.
24
25   The Budget is the City's revenue and expenses. As the Staff and Council go through the budgeting
26   process, they prioritize, but there is always a balance. For example, if 100% of revenues go toward
27   police service but nothing goes to roads, the police would not be able to get where they need to go.
28   There is always a balancing act between the different needs and wants of the City and its residents.
29
30   Staff is tasked with budgeting the City's restrained resources to its many needs. To do that, they
31   approach things differently than in a business. Income and expenses are broken into different Funds.


                                                       2
                            DRAFT – FOR DISCUSSION PURPOSES ONLY

                  BLUFFDALE CITY COUNCIL, LOCAL BUILDING AUTHORITY,
                  AND REDEVELOPMENT AGENCY BOARD MEETING MINUTES
                                 Wednesday, April 24, 2024

 1   The General Fund covers most of the City's services and operating expenses. The Water Fund looks
 2   and operates like a business, so its income statement looks like a business income statement. For
 3   example, the Water Fund Budget includes depreciation. There is no depreciation expense in the City's
 4   other Funds. The other various Funds are restricted in that they are set up to collect and expend money
 5   for very specific things. The money in those Funds cannot be spent on anything else.
 6
 7   With regard to priorities, one thing that has been highlighted in previous years is Fire Department
 8   salaries. Since the 2018-2019 Budget, the City Council has been working to improve Fire Department
 9   salaries in order to man the stations at an appropriate and safe level for both the firefighters and
10   residents.   Mr. Kartchner presented a chart depicting City growth.         Fire fees have increased
11   dramatically each year, proportionate to growth. Administrative Department costs have risen much
12   more slowly than the Fire Department because it is possible to leverage administration dollars over
13   more people as the City grows.
14
15   Both in the Budget Retreat and over the coming weeks as the Council identifies and priorities items
16   to focus on, the City Council will be considering requests and ranking them based on their level of
17   importance to the Council. The Tentative Budget is based on the direction of City Manager,
18   Mark Reid. His goal is to ensure that the Budget reflects the Council's requests, but it is from this
19   point forward that the Council will make its own determinations for the Final Budget.
20
21   As Staff goes through the budgeting process, they identify costs and revenues. The City provides
22   specific primary services like street cleaning and maintaining the parks. Some primary services are
23   recurring; for example, park restrooms must be cleaned, and garbage emptied weekly. Some primary
24   services occur less frequently; for example, recent flooding at one of the parks in Perry Farms. Some
25   services are discretionary, meaning they may or may not happen as funds permit.
26
27   Not all revenue sources are equal. Some, like property taxes, are recurring. Some are non-recurring;
28   for example, new developments pay one-time development and permitting fees. Property taxes are
29   the City's most stable revenue stream. Franchise fees related to energy costs are another somewhat
30   stable source of revenue but are slightly more volatile than property taxes. Other service fees include
31   street lighting, stormwater, and garbage collection. These items combined cover the City's basic

                                                       3
                             DRAFT – FOR DISCUSSION PURPOSES ONLY

                  BLUFFDALE CITY COUNCIL, LOCAL BUILDING AUTHORITY,
                  AND REDEVELOPMENT AGENCY BOARD MEETING MINUTES
                                 Wednesday, April 24, 2024

 1   expenses.
 2
 3   Slightly more volatile income sources include sales taxes, business licenses, court fines, and things of
 4   that nature. They go up and down quite a bit. For the last few years, sales taxes have been a stable
 5   form of review. However, in 2008-2010 when the economy crashed, cities that relied on sales tax
 6   revenue suffered because it dropped off significantly as people's buying habits changed.
 7
 8   The final component is development-related fees, which can be very volatile. When Mr. Reid first
 9   came to the City, they only had three building permits in a full year. Over the last few years, hundreds
10   of building permits have been pulled every year. Additional costs are associated with those specific
11   things that need to be covered.
12
13   Mr. Kartchner discussed budgeting basics. City budgets serve a different purpose than business
14   budgets, and as such the basic tenets of municipal budgeting differ from business budgeting. In
15   business, the budget is a goal, something they are trying to achieve. It may or may not be aggressive.
16   In government, the expenditures budget is called Appropriations. Rather than being a goal or forecast
17   of what they are expecting to spend, it is the maximum amount they are allowed to spend.
18
19   At the end of the year, if the City spends less than budgeted, it doesn't mean they were sandbagging
20   or expecting to make more or spend less. It's just that that was the maximum they could spend and
21   what they were expecting to spend, but for whatever reason they did not. An example is a previous
22   year when the Fire Department could not fill open positions; $500,000 of its salaries budget was left
23   unspent at the end of the year due to the vacancies.
24
25   By State law, the City Budget is balanced. That balancing must include an unappropriated Fund
26   balance of 5% to 35%. At the end of the year, part of a balanced Budget includes having those
27   reserves available. In preparing this year's Budget, Mr. Kartchner reviewed another city's budget
28   documents. That city has a goal to maintain its unappropriated Fund balance at between 30% and
29   35%. If it drops below that level, they are required to specifically address the shortfall and discuss
30   their plans to bring it back to the requirement.
31

 1   Finance Director, Stephanie Thayer, provided additional details.            At the Budget Retreat, all
 2   department heads presented their requests for the upcoming Budget year. All those requests are
 3   included in the draft Budget. The BRC reviewed and provided feedback on how the data could be
 4   better analyzed and presented with charts, graphs, and narratives, which have been added to the draft.
 5   The Budget will continue to be refined over the next six weeks as new revenue estimates become
 6   available. Currently, the Tentative Budget has a large use of Fund balance, so they will be working
 7   to limit that use as much as possible prior to final Budget approval.
 8
 9   A letter from Mr. Reid was included with the meeting packet that explains the methodology used. It
10   points out that the City is a service organization, so the bulk of its expenditures are in personnel costs.
11   Included in the Tentative Budget is the hiring of several new employees: two patrol officers, five Full-
12   Time Equivalent ("FTE") employees in the Public Works Department, and upgrading two Fire
13   Department positions from part-time to full-time.
14
15   Bluffdale is a growing community, and with growth comes the need for new and expanded
16   infrastructure. Growth also impacts the replacement cycle of the City's current equipment and
17   infrastructure. The Capital Projects Fund includes $8 million for these new and ongoing projects.
18   Additionally, $35 million in new and ongoing projects will be paid by money allocated by the state,
19   grants from state and county sources, and shared projects such as the 14400 South project.
20
21   The Budget also includes several hundred thousand dollars for recreation and sports programs, Old
22   West Days activities, Bluffdale arts events, the Miss Bluffdale scholarship program, Healthy
23   Bluffdale promotions, and various other events.
24
25   The City's underlying approach has been and continues to be a conservative one. The aim is to be
26   fiscally responsible and financially sustainable while meeting the future and current needs of the City.
27
28   Ms. Thayer provided an overview of the Tentative Budget which incorporates the recommendation
29   of the Budget Review Committee to include charts, graphs, historical data, and narratives.
30   Mr. Kartchner added that some BRC recommendations were adjusted, and others were not
31   incorporated due to time constraints. As updated Budgets are issued over the next several weeks,

 1   more of their suggestions will be included.
 2
 3   Regarding revenues, Mr. Kartchner stated that historically sales taxes have grown at a rapid rate.
 4   Based on available year-to-date information, sales tax revenue is approximate as budgeted for Fiscal
 5   Year 2024, and 2025 is expected to have the same or slightly lower revenue. Those projections were
 6   created using a Seasonal Auto-Regressive Integrated Moving Average Model ("SARIMA")
 7   regression analysis, which evaluates increases and decreases over time, as well as the seasonality of
 8   sales taxes. Staff performed back-testing to gauge the program's performance, and at a 95%
 9   confidence interval, the analysis predicts accurately.
10
11   Mr. Reid added that information was provided at both the City Managers Association Conference and
12   the Utah League of Cities and Towns (“ULCT”) Conference indicating that sales tax revenue will
13   decrease in 2025 compared to other years. That will reduce the City's ability to expend funds because
14   revenues will be down.
15
16   Ms. Thayer indicated that the actual property tax number will not be available until June, and it will
17   be added to the Budget at that time. Mr. Kartchner stated that it usually comes in immediately before
18   the final Budget is due, so it always needs to be added immediately prior to final Budget approval.
19   Ms. Thayer pointed out that the revenue side of the Budget is as important as the expenses. She
20   reported that the Legal Department is adding an Administrative Citation Enforcement ("ACE")
21   program, which increases that Budget by 20%.
22
23   Mr. Kartchner mentioned that both residents and the BRC requested that the percentage change from
24   the previous year's numbers be included in the Budget. Because some actual numbers are delayed,
25   the Budget includes both the change from the projection and the change from the prior year's Budget.
26
27   Ms. Thayer indicated that both an overview of each Fund and more detailed information are included
28   with the Budget packet. Funds include Class C Roads, Community Events, Economic Development
29   Area ("EDA"), and Redevelopment Agency ("RDA") Funds. She indicated that some EDA/RDAs
30   are expiring. Mr. Kartchner added that Jordan Narrows EDA has expired, and the revenue shown is
31   anticipated earned interest on the balance. The other two listed will expire within the next two years.

 2   Ms. Thayer continued the Budget overview. Impact Fee revenue categories include Parks, Public
 3   Safety, Roads and Bridges, and Storm Drains.
 4
 5   Capital Projects are summarized based on revenue source. Expenditures include City Projects and
 6   Equipment, which are initiated and paid for by the City with contributions from the General Fund and
 7   use of Fund balance. Other governments including state, county, or other government entities
 8   provided contributions, for example, for the railroad crossing bridge at 14400 South. Mr. Kartchner
 9   added that that bridge is the biggest item on the Capital Projects list, and existing allocated state funds
10   will pay for most of it. Grant Related Projects include both fully and partially reimbursed projects.
11   Shared Projects include some projects that the City is a pass-through for, such as 14400 in front of
12   City Hall. Last is the Miscellaneous category.
13
14   The Water Fund category includes revenues, expenses, and Impact Fees. Local Building Authority
15   includes both City Hall and the Public Works Building construction. Fire and Police Protection Fund
16   includes some of the requested increases.
17
18   Regarding the detailed Tentative Budget, there are columns for the Prior Year Actual, the current
19   budget ending June 30, 2024, the most recent completed period ending March 31, departmental
20   requests for FY 2025, and a five-year projection for each line item that is for reference only.
21
22   The following assumptions were used in creating the Budget:
23
24      •   Inflation: 3%
25      •   Population growth: 1%
26      •   CPI increases: 3%
27      •   Building permits: Best Estimate
28      •   Benefits renewal:
29              o Medical: 4.1%
30              o Dental: 4.7%
31              o Vision: No increase

 1
 2   Ms. Thayer provided an overview of Capital Projects. The largest expenditures are road projects,
 3   including roundabouts at 13800 South and the intersection of 3600 West and 14000 South, and
 4   ongoing road maintenance as recommended by City Engineer, Michael Fazio. Mr. Kartchner
 5   indicated that the amount shown is in addition to the amount allocated in the Class C Road Fund. The
 6   City first spends the allocated Class C funds, then the allocated Capital Projects funds. The City's
 7   portion of reconstruction and utilities for 14400 South is included. South Valley Sewer District’s
 8   portion of that project is $6.7 million. Capital Projects are one-time costs. Additional projects may
 9   come up and need to be addressed midyear.
10
11   Other Governmental is large projects that the state and county provide funding for, such as the railroad
12   crossing on 14600 South. Grant-Related Capital Projects include the rodeo arena. Estimated Future
13   Capital Projects are included as well. The Capital Projects Fund revenue comes from contributions
14   from the General Fund, the use of Fund balance, governmental and state monies, and grants.
15
16   Ms. Thayer also gave an overview of the Fire and Police Protection Fund, which includes all property
17   tax revenue as well as an additional contribution from the General Fund. Other revenue sources
18   include the Wildland Fire Fees and a Public Safety Fee. Mr. Reid stated that a group is sent out to
19   fight wildland fires, and they are reimbursed for a specific amount. Employees are paid from those
20   fees, and the City nets approximately 10 percent of the amount. For example, the Budget includes a
21   total revenue for that category of $200,000 and a total expense of $100,000. Ten percent, or $20,000,
22   is revenue to the City. Those numbers are estimates. Mr. Kartchner added that the amount is lower
23   than the previous year because the state has changed its reimbursement process.
24
25   Ms. Thayer indicated that some of the equipment listed in the tentative Budget will be paid using one-
26   time American Rescue Plan Act ("ARPA") funds. Mr. Kartchner gave the example of a dump truck
27   being one-time funds because the truck will last ten years. The Police Department purchases at least
28   three trucks every year to keep the fleet at the required level. The definition is one-time funds, but in
29   actuality, three trucks per year is a recurring cost.
30
31   There is a reappropriated Fund balance of $360,000. Staff anticipates transferring that balance to

 1   3.       Mayor and Council Reports.
 2
 3   Mayor Hall reported on the following:
 4
 5        •   It is National Library Week. She visited all six Bluffdale elementary schools, including the
 6            virtual elementary school, and read to the students.
 7        •   The Virtual Academy, which includes elementary, middle, and high schools, for the Jordan
 8            School District had an art show.
 9        •   She attended meetings regarding Google Fiber and the Zoo and Arts and Parks ("ZAP") tax,
10            as well as a meeting of the Utah Transit Authority ("UTA") Advisory Board.
11        •   She visited several businesses, including an olive oil business that recently opened; Custom
12            Events, which has been in Sandy for 50 years; a paragliding company, an organization
13            company; and Stotz Equipment, which is a sponsor for City events this year.
14        •   She participated in a Ribbon Cutting at the Adaptive Arena, an indoor arena for people of all
15            abilities. She encouraged everyone who knows children who may benefit from it to invite
16            them to reach out to the Arena. It was a fabulous event.
17        •   She attended the Sandy City Fire Station groundbreaking with Fire Chief, Mark Evans, and
18            City Council Member Aston. They spoke with Mayor Monica Zontanski about the support
19            they have from their residents, who voted for a $21 million bond to fund the new station. The
20            new station will be state of the art and will include training facilities. She is excited for them.

 6   Mayor Hall provided background on the districting discussion. She has lived in Bluffdale for 18

 8   this Council consider districting as well. She clarified that the City Council cannot take action on
 9   districting until it has been discussed in public, but the discussion does not mean that the Council is
10   interested or uninterested in creating districts. They cannot discuss an issue if no research has been
11   done, so Staff was asked to research both the law regarding districting and what it might look like.
12   Maps were created for both five districts and four districts with one at-large member. The Mayor is
13   always an at-large position. The topic was discussed on April 10, and they committed as a Council

15   amended Agenda was issued to include it. Unfortunately, the option of having four districts and one
16   at-large member was also missing from the meeting packet.

20   questions at the meeting. She proposed possibly including an article in the newsletter or putting out a
21   survey but wanted to see where the discussion led.

24   lot of great arguments on both sides. The City has a responsibility to consider the interests of
25   everybody in Bluffdale, regardless of whether they vote. He does not like that there are no council
26   members from the Independence area, and therefore half the population of Bluffdale does not have
27   representation. The City Council has the responsibility to hear everybody's voice and interests, and
28   citizens from different areas of the City have vastly different interests. He noticed that a majority of
29   residents from the west side of Bluffdale are not interested in districting whereas east side residents
30   are interested in it, and knows that a time will come when those same residents are arguing the

14          8.1     Resolution 2024-27 - Adopting the Tentative Budget for the 2024-2025 Fiscal
15                  Year and establishing the Time and Place for the Public Hearing on the Final
16                  Budget for the 2024-2025 Fiscal Year. (Staff Presenters, Stephanie Thayer and
17                  Bruce Kartchner) [LBA & RDA Public Hearing held in conjunction with the
18                  Budget Hearing].
19
20   Mayor Hall indicated that there had been many Council Work Sessions regarding the 2024-2025
21   Budget, as well as a Budget Retreat where they heard from every department. Earlier in the meeting,
22   there was a presentation regarding the budget process and a presentation from the BRC chair.
23
24   Mr. Kartchner indicated that in creating the Budget, Staff reviewed the needs of the City. They had
25   input from all departments as to their needs to maintain or improve the current service level. The
26   Police Department and Fire Department both requested an expansion of services to a higher level,
27   which includes increased expenses.
28
29   Next, they projected revenues. Some revenues are projected to be lower and more uncertain than in
30   the past. There were years when Staff was very confident in development fees, for example, because
31   big developers were coming in with large, multiple-home projects, but now the amount of available
32   land for such projects is diminishing. There is a reduction in those fees, but at present the reduction
33   in housing is being offset somewhat by an increase in commercial. Businesses and commercial


                                                       21
                              DRAFT – FOR DISCUSSION PURPOSES ONLY

                  BLUFFDALE CITY COUNCIL, LOCAL BUILDING AUTHORITY,
                  AND REDEVELOPMENT AGENCY BOARD MEETING MINUTES
                                 Wednesday, April 24, 2024

 1   enterprises see Bluffdale as a good place to be right now because of the location and availability of
 2   services.
 3
 4   Sales tax revenues are sloping off. Staff did know all the reasons behind this change, but it may be
 5   due to inflation. Inflation has slowed to 3, but costs are 20% higher than in 2021, and those added
 6   costs are being reflected in residents' spending habits.       Wages have also increased, but the
 7   simultaneously elevated costs are causing changes in spending habits. As additional businesses come
 8   in, they bring in additional sales tax revenue and commercial property taxes, but that doesn't
 9   necessarily offset the associated additional costs. For example, the City will need to hire additional
10   police officers to patrol new businesses. Costs are being driven up, and as they go up, they must be
11   addressed accordingly.
12
13   The overall Budget is relatively consistent with the previous year, with the exception of the increase
14   to the Fire and Police Protection Fund. Mr. Kartchner reminded the Council that the Budget is
15   tentative. Multiple changes will be made and presented to the Council over the coming weeks. If the
16   Council has questions or would like to have public conversations about additional topics, that can be
17   done.
18
19   Currently, the General Fund is showing a use of Fund balance of over $800,000. In Mr. Kartchner's
20   opinion, that number is too high, so Staff will work to reduce it. One challenge is that some revenue
21   numbers are months in arrears. For example, only six months of sales tax revenue collections are
22   available and must be used to project for the rest of the year and into 2025. They are using artificial
23   intelligence to help facilitate those projections. From his viewpoint, the City has been both lucky and
24   not lucky over the past few years. Sales tax revenue has been increasing at a much faster rate than
25   expected, but it is now slowing, and the City has to determine how to handle that change.
26
27   Mr. Reid commented that during COVID-19, cities realized that the previous years' data was
28   irrelevant in setting a sales tax number. It was decided that sales tax should be kept the same as the
29   previous year, minus 40 percent. That caused cities to use reserves or cut expenses, to use their rainy-
30   day funds. In regard to the current Bluffdale budget, it is not raining; it is a normal yearly Budget.
31   Sales tax revenues softening is not cause for panic or to use of reserves until they strengthen.

                                                       22
                              DRAFT – FOR DISCUSSION PURPOSES ONLY

                  BLUFFDALE CITY COUNCIL, LOCAL BUILDING AUTHORITY,
                  AND REDEVELOPMENT AGENCY BOARD MEETING MINUTES
                                 Wednesday, April 24, 2024

 1   Mr. Kartchner reiterated that Staff will be working to reduce the use of Fund balance to an acceptable
 2   level. The Council can then review and provide input on their recommendations.
 3
 4   In response to a question from Mayor Hall, Mr. Kartchner indicated that the Fire and Police Protection
 5   Fund deficit is for equipment purchases. The two new police vehicles, type six fire truck, and
 6   equipment for the type one engine will be moved to Capital Projects. Additionally, he noted that a
 7   Public Safety Fee has been added to the Budget, which will help cover the increased Police and Fire
 8   Protection Fund costs.
 9
10   Mayor Hall indicated that the police contract increased significantly, and it must be covered. The
11   City needs more than two officers. She met with the Police Department, and all officers were
12   concerned about their safety. Officers were having to go to domestic and calls by themselves, and
13   one officer went to a shooting call on his own. It's unacceptable. Big businesses will not come to
14   Bluffdale unless it has better public safety.
15
16   Mr. Kartchner indicated his concern regarding upcoming commercial properties, a number of which
17   will require additional police assistance. Hotels, particularly extended-stay hotels, tend to require
18   more assistance from both police and fire. Staff is hoping a new grocery store will be built in the near
19   future, which will bring in additional revenue, but not enough to cover the associated additional costs.
20   The budgeting process includes five-year projections to help determine what needs to be done now to
21   ensure the City can cover that future expansion.
22
23   Council Member Wilding commented that the Police Chief's presentation included a mention that a
24   new police officer was requested four years previously. He believes the City is doing a good job of
25   being careful and conscious with the Budget, but it is time to solve that problem.
26
27   Mr. Kartchner stated that historically the Budget has been very conservative relative to the
28   surrounding cities. From a financial standpoint, not a lot can be controlled at the City level, but one
29   thing that can be controlled is property taxes. Bluffdale has the second-lowest property tax in the
30   entire valley, which indicates that the City is using its available funds wisely. That is particularly
31   important when you consider that Bluffdale is largely a bedroom community with large swaths of


                                                        23
                              DRAFT – FOR DISCUSSION PURPOSES ONLY

                  BLUFFDALE CITY COUNCIL, LOCAL BUILDING AUTHORITY,
                  AND REDEVELOPMENT AGENCY BOARD MEETING MINUTES
                                 Wednesday, April 24, 2024

 1   low-density areas. The cost per population of providing services for large lots is much higher than
 2   for smaller lots. Smaller lots in other areas generate more net income for the city, particularly with
 3   online sales taxes. Higher-density populations generate a lot of sales tax revenue. With the number
 4   of large lots, one would expect Bluffdale to have one of the highest property tax rates in the county,
 5   not the second lowest.
 6
 7   Fortunately, additional commercial is coming in that is assessed at a higher rate and also generates
 8   franchise fees. For example, data centers don't have a lot of traffic, so they don't cause wear and tear
 9   on infrastructure, but they use a lot of electricity that generates a power franchise fee.
10
11   Mayor Hall opened the public hearing.
12
13   Japheth McGee reported that he is a Financial Advisor to local governments. In that process, he often
14   talks about ratings. Every year, bond rating agencies post medians from around the country indicating
15   what fund balances and property value per capita should be for cities of different sizes. They give
16   examples of both highly and low-rated cities. Consistently in those reports, fund balances are
17   increasing. It is not a recession like 2008 when sales taxes decreased, and cities saw hardships. As a
18   resident, he does not want to see a high use of Fund balance this year because when a hard time comes,
19   it will be difficult for the City to make that transition if some of the Fund balance has been used. He
20   hopes the City does not use Fund balance during good times.
21
22   Erik Swanson voiced his support for increased monies for public safety. More full-time Police and
23   Fire positions will allow for consistent coverage.
24
25   There were no additional public comments. The public hearing was closed.
26
27   Council Member Crockett thanked the staff for being conservative on the Budget. She believes that
28   over the last couple of years, the City has gotten serious about funding Fire and Police. She hears
29   comments about funding Fire and Police first, but she has not heard viable options on what other
30   items can be cut to cover those expenses. She also believes the rainy-day fund should not be used.
31
32   Council Member Aston stated that once the Council Members approve the Tentative Budget, it will


                                                          24
                             DRAFT – FOR DISCUSSION PURPOSES ONLY

                  BLUFFDALE CITY COUNCIL, LOCAL BUILDING AUTHORITY,
                  AND REDEVELOPMENT AGENCY BOARD MEETING MINUTES
                                 Wednesday, April 24, 2024

 1   be time to determine what can be changed.
 2
 3   Council Member Austin expressed gratitude for Staff's efforts in creating the Budget. He looked
 4   forward to working with Ms. Thayer, Mr. Kartchner, and Mr. Reid toward the final Budget. He is a
 5   firm believer in taking care of needs first, and he believes it is important emergency services get what
 6   they need for the City. He is not in favor of added fees, but he understands that the Budget is tentative
 7   and looks forward to working to find other solutions.
 8
 9   Council Member Lord had a conversation with Messrs. Reid and Kartchner earlier in the day. He
10   was unsure what was meant by "Tentative" Budget, but he understands now. He will follow up with
11   Staff so he can be better informed as they move forward with the process.

30   Member Austin. Vote on motion: Board Member Hall-Yes, Chair Crockett-Yes, Board
31   Member Lord-Yes, Board Member Austin-Yes, Board Member Aston-Yes, Board Member
32   Wilding-Yes. The motion passed unanimously.
33
34   Chair Crockett stated that she would like to meet with Community and Economic Development
35   Director, Grant Crowell, to talk about available funds in the RDA account and any possibility of using
36   those funds for the FrontRunner station. Mayor Hall asked if the City could start on a Station Area
37   Plan before the environmental study is done. Chair Crockett indicated that she wants to stay on top


                                                      26
                              DRAFT – FOR DISCUSSION PURPOSES ONLY

                    BLUFFDALE CITY COUNCIL, LOCAL BUILDING AUTHORITY,
                    AND REDEVELOPMENT AGENCY BOARD MEETING MINUTES
                                   Wednesday, April 24, 2024

 1   of it, but it may be too early.
 2
 3   Mr. Crowell responded that the Station Area Plan is a subset of the General Plan, and there is never a
 4   wrong time to take a look at an area of the General Plan. Formally, there is no station, even though
 5   $250 million is funded for one. It is not on the Regional Transportation Plan and environmental is
 6   not finished, but a discussion regarding what it might look like and what the implications might be is
 7   appropriate. Regarding when to spend RDA money and what to spend it for, Mr. Crowell indicated
 8   that he had recently asked Mr. Kartchner and other Staff members about that. All of Bluffdale
 9   Boulevard is in Eastern Bluffdale EDA, and infrastructure is a valid use of that Fund. The City also
10   wants to make sure it isn't paying the Utah Department of Transportation's share of the costs.
11
12   Land use implications could be discussed at any time. When the Station Area Plan is formalized and
13   there is a better understanding of how it might impact the Housing Plan, a more targeted discussion
14   can be held.
15
16   Council Member Aston stated that it would be beneficial to the Council to hear more about the RDA
17   funds and their appropriate usage. Mayor Hall stated that a pre-station area discussion will be added
18   to the agenda. She added that, per HB-462, a Station Area Plan with high-density housing is required
19   around a FrontRunner station. Mr. Crowell indicated that up-to-date information is available at the
20   Wasatch Front Regional Council ("WFRC") website. The WFRC is required to participate in and
21   certify plans. When all the information is in, the City will create a robust plan, and they will need
22   consulting help with the staff, field trips, etc.

 9   Public Works Director, Shane Paddock, provided an update on the new Public Works Building. It is

27   used. Mr. Reid added that the two Jordan School District schools are in Day Ranch, and there is a trail
28   through the rear of Independence by the canal. The City received permission to build a bridge over
29   the canal. Mayor Hall stated that she has been working to schedule a ribbon cutting. She will
30   coordinate with the Council and Staff.

Bluffdale City Audit Committee Charter

Audit Committee Authority
Pursuant to resolution number 2023-30, dated December 13, 2023, the Bluffdale City
Council of Bluffdale City has established an audit committee to assist the Bluffdale City
Council in the oversight of the external audit functions.

Mission
The Bluffdale City Council of Bluffdale City, Utah has established an audit committee to
provide independent advice, assistance, and recommendations to the Bluffdale City
Council in the oversight of the City’s financial reporting processes, internal controls and
external audit functions of Bluffdale City.

Composition and Requisite Skills
The Bluffdale City Audit Committee is comprised of three (3) members. This ensures
that investigations regarding the work of management and external auditors remain
confidential until reports are made public to the governing body. The committee shall
include: Three (3) members as appointed by the Mayor of Bluffdale City and approved
by the Bluffdale City Council as established by 2024-09.
The Committee members collectively should possess the knowledge in accounting,
auditing, and financial reporting needed to understand and evaluate Bluffdale City
financial statements and the external audit activities. Accordingly, the Bluffdale City
Audit Committee’s members, collectively, should:
   1) Possess the requisite knowledge necessary to understand technical and complex
      financial reporting issues.
   2) Have the ability to communicate with auditors, public finance officers and the
      governing body.
   3) Be knowledgeable about internal controls, financial statement audits and
      management/operational audits.
          a. If no audit committee members have sufficient personal internal control or
             finance knowledge, the committee must gain this knowledge via a financial
             expert (either volunteer or paid) advisor.
                  i. The financial expert advisor must:
                        1. Be independent of management
                        2. Be present for meetings
                        3. Not be a member of the audit committee
                        4. Not vote on committee actions
Organization
The Bluffdale City Audit Committee shall annually elect from among its members a
member to serve as: (1) the Chair; (2) Vice Chair; and (3) Secretary of the Committee.

Duties and Responsibilities
The duties and responsibilities of the Bluffdale City Audit Committee include the
following:
   1) External Audit Focus
          a. Provide recommendations regarding the selection of the external auditor
             whether on an incumbent basis or through managing the Request for
             Proposal (“RFP”) process on an as needed basis.
          b. The Bluffdale City Audit Committee shall perform an RFP process, for the
             selection of an external auditor, at a minimum of every five (5) years or as
             otherwise deemed necessary in the opinion of the Bluffdale Audit
             Committee or the Bluffdale City Council.
          c. Meet with the external auditor prior to commencement of the audit to,
             among other things, review the engagement letter.
          d. Review and discuss with the external auditor any risk assessment of the
             entity’s fiscal operations developed as part of the auditor’s responsibilities
             under governmental auditing standards for a financial statement audit and
             federal single audit standards, if applicable.
          e. Receive and review the draft annual audit report and accompanying draft
             management letter, including the external auditor’s assessment of the
             entity’s system of internal controls, and, working directly with the external
             auditor, assist the Bluffdale City Council in interpreting such documents.
          f. Make a recommendation to the Bluffdale City Council on accepting the
             annual audit report.
          g. Review every corrective action plan developed by Bluffdale City
             management and assist the Bluffdale City Council in the implementation of
             such plans.
   2) Internal Audit Focus
          a. As of the effective date of the adoption of this Bluffdale City Audit
             Committee Charter, Bluffdale City management and the Bluffdale City
             Council have determined that Bluffdale City does not have the current
             resources and ability to establish a useful and effective internal audit
             function.
          b. As a result of item 2) a., the Bluffdale City Audit Committee has no current
             duties and responsibilities with regards to internal audit functions for
             Bluffdale City.
          c. In the event that Bluffdale City management and the Bluffdale City Council
             further determines that it has the resources and ability to create an internal
                                                                                             2
              audit function for Bluffdale City, this Bluffdale City Audit Charter shall be
              amended and approved accordingly and establish duties and
              responsibilities of the Bluffdale City Audit Committee with regards to the
              internal audit functions.
   3) Administrative and Other Matters
          a. Hold regularly scheduled meetings.
          b. Review and revise the Audit Committee Charter no less than once every
             five (5) years, or as necessary.
          c. Establish procedures for the receipt, retention and treatment of complaints
             regarding the City’s accounting and internal controls. Such procedures
             shall be referred to as Whistle Blower complaints and procedures.
          d. Monitor financial controls performed by City management, including,
             without limitation, financial controls designed to detect and prevent
             management override of other financial controls.
   4) Chair
          a. Conduct meetings.
          b. Retrieve and disseminate complaints from designated sources.
          c. Provide written and oral reports to the Bluffdale City Council as applicable.
   5) Vice Chair
          a. Conduct meetings in the absence of the Chair.
   6) Secretary
          a. Maintain an accurate record of meeting minutes.
          b. Coordinate with City staff the preparation and notice of agendas for
             meetings.

Membership
The membership duties of the Bluffdale City Audit Committee include the following:
   1) Good Faith – Members of the Committee shall perform their duties in good faith,
      in a manner they reasonably believe to be in the best interests of the Committee
      and Bluffdale City with such care as a generally prudent person in a similar
      position would use under similar circumstances.
   2) Independence – An individual may not serve on an audit committee if he or she:
          a. Is employed by the entity (other than governing board members).
          b. Currently provides, or within the prior two years, has provided, goods or
             services to the entity.
          c. Is a family member of an employee or officer.
          d. Is the owner of or has a direct and material interest in a company
             providing goods or services to the entity.

                                                                                              3
   3) Confidentiality – During the exercise of duties and responsibilities, the Committee
      members may have access to confidential information. The Committee shall
      have an obligation to Bluffdale City to maintain the confidentiality of such
      information.
   4) Term of Service – The initial current selection of three (3) members by the
      Bluffdale City Mayor and approved by Bluffdale City Council, resolution number
      2024-09, shall have staggered terms of service. One member shall have a one
      (1) year term of service, another member shall have a two (2) year term of
      service and another member shall have a three (3) year term of service. On the
      expiration of a committee member’s term of service, the Bluffdale City Mayor
      may re-appoint the expiring member to another term of service or participate in a
      selection process for a different member, and the resulting selected member is
      then approved by the Bluffdale City Council. After the initial current selection of
      three (3) members, resolution number 2024-09 provides for a three-year term of
      service for appointed and approved Committee members. Members may be
      removed by a two-thirds (2/3) vote of the Bluffdale City Council or at the
      recommendation of the mayor and a simple majority of the Bluffdale City Council.
      Vacancies occurring through expiration of terms of the appointment, death,
      disability, resignation, moving from Bluffdale City or removal by the Bluffdale City
      Council, if applicable, shall be filled by appointment by the mayor, with the advice
      and consent of the Bluffdale City Council.
   5) No member of the Bluffdale Audit Committee shall receive compensation for their
      service.
   6) Bluffdale City Budget Review Committee – Pursuant to resolution 2024-10, dated
      January 10, 2024, the initial members appointed pursuant to resolution 2024-09,
      to the Bluffdale City Audit Committee, shall also be members of the Bluffdale City
      Budget Review Committee.

Meetings and Notification
The Bluffdale City Audit Committee shall meet a minimum of three (3) times each year
with any additional meetings scheduled on an as needed basis. An agenda of each
meeting should be clearly determined in advance and the Audit Committee should
receive supporting documents in advance, for reasonable review and consideration.
The Audit Committee shall create meeting minutes which include the meeting:
   1)   Agenda
   2)   Time, date, and location
   3)   Attendance
   4)   Findings requiring further investigation
   5)   Items to report to the governing body




                                                                                         4
Decision-Making Process
All decisions shall be reached by vote of a simple majority of the total membership of
the committee. A quorum constitutes a simple majority of the total membership and
meetings will not be conducted unless a quorum is present.

Reporting Requirements
The Bluffdale City Audit Committee has the duty and responsibility to report its activities
to the Bluffdale City Council as needed, but not less than annually. Periodic written
reports of Audit Committee activities are an important communication link between the
Audit Committee and the Bluffdale City Council on key decisions and responsibilities.
The Audit Committee’s reporting requirements are to:
   1)   Report on the scope and breadth of committee activities so that the Bluffdale City
        Council is kept informed of its work.
   2)   Provide minutes or a summary of minutes of meetings which clearly record the
        actions and recommendations of the Committee.
   3)   Report on their review of the Bluffdale City draft annual audit report and
        accompanying management letter and their review of significant findings. This
        report shall include a specific statement that the Bluffdale City Audit Committee
        has discussed the financial statements (a) with management; (b) with the City’s
        independent auditors in private; and (c) privately between Bluffdale City Audit
        Committee members.
   4)   Report on suspected fraud, waste or abuse, or significant internal control findings
        and activities of the internal control function.
   5)   Report on indications of material or significant non-compliances with laws or
        Bluffdale City policies and regulations.
   6)   Report on any other matters that the committee believes should be disclosed to
        the Bluffdale City Council.

Charter Review
The Bluffdale City Audit Committee shall assess and report to the Bluffdale City Council
on the adequacy of this Charter no less than once every five (5) years or as the
Bluffdale City Audit Committee and the Bluffdale City Council deem necessary. Charter
modifications, as recommended by the Audit Committee, should be presented to the
Bluffdale City Council in writing for their review and action.

Bluffdale City Budget Review Committee
Charter

Budget Review Committee Authority
Pursuant to resolution number 2023-31, dated December 13, 2023, the Bluffdale City
Council (“Council”) of Bluffdale City (“City”) has established a Budget Review Committee
(“Committee”) to review the City’s annual budget and make recommendations to improve
the content, transparency, and clarity of the budget document.

Mission
The Bluffdale City Council of Bluffdale City, Utah has established a committee to review
the annual budget and make recommendations to improve, the content, the transparency
and clarity of the budget document to the Bluffdale Mayor, City Council, and residents.

Composition and Requisite Skills
The Committee is comprised of not less than five (5) and not more than seven (7)
members. Members are appointed by the Mayor, with the advice and consent of the
Council.
The Committee members shall be Bluffdale residents, city staff, or Council members.
Committee members collectively should possess a background in finance or accounting
and have a basic understanding of government financial reporting and auditing as
established by resolution 2023-31. Accordingly, Committee members, collectively,
should:
   1) Have the ability to communicate financial topics to City residents, Mayor, and the
      Council.
   2) Be knowledgeable about fund accounting, governmental budgets, and
      communication of complex financial topics.
          a. If no budget review committee members have sufficient finance
              knowledge, the committee must gain this knowledge via a financial expert
              (either volunteer or paid) advisor.
                   i. The financial expert advisor must:
                         1. Be present for meetings
                         2. Not be a member of the budget review committee
                         3. Not vote on committee actions
   3) Strive to understand the goals and objectives of the Mayor and Council.
   4) Strive to understand budgetary concerns of Bluffdale City residents.
   5) A good working relationship with City finance staff.
Organization
The Committee shall annually elect from among its members a member to serve as: (1)
the Chair; (2) Vice Chair; and (3) Secretary of the Committee.

Duties and Responsibilities
The duties and responsibilities of the Committee include the following:
   1) Assist in the review and recommendation of annual budgets to the Mayor and
      Council.
   2) Review and analyze revenue projections, expenditure requests, staff
      compensation structures, and departmental budget justifications.
   3) Recommend and review fiscal health targets.
   4) Assist in creating transparent, concise, and informative financial summaries and
      graphics for presentation to the Mayor, Council, and City residents.
   5) Propose recommendations for budget adjustments and improvements.
   6) Periodically review outsourced staff expenditures and make recommendations.
   7) Provide recommendations on the budget process to the Mayor and Council to
      foster transparency and facilitate the Mayor and Council’s ability to make key
      decisions.
   8) Approve committee meeting minutes via a quorum.
   9) Chair
          a. Conduct meetings.
          b. Solicit agenda items from committee members and City staff in advance of
             meetings.
          c. Disseminate supporting documents in advance of meetings to provide a
             reasonable period to review.
                    i. Make presentations to the Mayor and Council on decisions and
                       actions of the Committee. The Chair may appoint a designee to
                       fulfill the above responsibility.
   10) Vice Chair
          a. Fulfill the role of Chair in the absence of the Chair.
   11) Secretary
          a. Maintain an accurate record of meeting minutes including
             recommendations that will be made to the Mayor and Council.
          b. Coordinate with City staff the preparation and notice of agendas for
             meetings.

Membership
The membership duties of the Committee include the following:


                                                                                         2
   1) Good Faith – Members of the Committee shall perform their duties in good faith,
      in a manner they reasonably believe to be in the best interests of Bluffdale City
      with such care as a generally prudent person in a similar position would use
      under similar circumstances.
   2) Confidentiality – During the exercise of duties and responsibilities, the Committee
      members may have access to confidential information. The Committee shall
      have an obligation to Bluffdale City to maintain the confidentiality of such
      information, as applicable in accordance with open meeting statutes.
   3) Term of Service – The initial current selection of (3) members by the Bluffdale
      City Mayor and approved by Bluffdale City Council, resolution number 2023-31,
      shall have staggered terms of service. Three (3) members shall have a one (1)
      year term of service, two (2) members shall have a two (2) year term of service
      and one (1) member shall have a three (3) year term of service. On the expiration
      of a Committee member’s term of service, the Bluffdale City Mayor may re-
      appoint the expiring member to another term of service or participate in a
      selection process for a different member, and the resulting selected member is
      then approved by the Bluffdale City Council. After the initial current selection of
      members, resolution number 2023-31 provides for a three-year term of service
      for appointed and approved Committee members.
   4) Removal – Members may be removed by a two-thirds vote of the Council.

Meetings and Notification
The Bluffdale City Budget Review Committee shall meet quarterly with additional
meetings scheduled on an as needed basis. An agenda of each meeting should be clearly
determined in advance and the Budget Review Committee should receive supporting
documents in advance, for reasonable review and consideration.
The Budget Review Committee shall create meeting minutes which include the meeting:
   1)   Agenda
   2)   Time, date, and location
   3)   Attendance
   4)   Action items
   5)   Items to report to the Mayor and Council

Decision-Making Process
All decisions shall be reached by vote of a simple majority of the total membership of the
committee. A quorum constitutes a simple majority of the total membership and no
binding action can occur unless a quorum is present.

Charter Review
The Committee shall assess and report to the Mayor and Council on the adequacy of this
Charter each even numbered year or as necessary. Charter modifications, as
recommended by the Committee, should be presented to the Mayor and Council in writing
for their review and action.

                                      MEMORANDUM

To:   Bluffdale City Council
From: Fredric Donaldson, Bluffdale City Attorney
Date: May 13, 2024
Re:   Indigent Defense Services Agreement with Larsen, Larsen, Nash & Larsen


        Pursuant to Utah Code § 77-32-101 et seq. and the 6th Amendment of the United
State Constitution, the City of Bluffdale (“City”) is obligated to provide qualified,
independent indigent defense counsel to persons who are charged with violation of laws
where there is a potential for incarceration.
        In 2017, the City entered into a contract with the law firm of Larsen, Larsen, Nash &
Larsen (“The Larsen law firm”) to provide legal defense services for indigent defendants.
The City awarded the contract on the basis of demonstrated competence and qualification
at a fair and reasonable price.
        The City recognizes that appointed defense counsel must be free to defend clients
zealously and without fear of termination, reduction in compensation, reduction in staff or
reduction in defense resources and the proposed agreement provides for and ensures such
representation
         The Larsen law firm has requested an increase in rates related to indigent defense
services and the City has determined that the requested increase is reasonable in light of
current market rates and conditions and the services that have been and will be provided.
        The rates have not increased since 2017 and the rates will be consistent until such
time as the contract is terminated or a new agreement negotiated between the parties.
        The draft agreement approved by the parties is attached hereto as Exhibit A.
Exhibit A

                                 RESOLUTION NO. 2024-37

                   A RESOLUTION AUTHORIZING THE CITY MANAGER
            TO ENTER INTO AN AGREEMENT FOR INDIGENT DEFENSE SERVICES

WHEREAS, Bluffdale City (“City”) is a political subdivision of the State of Utah required to

law;
WHEREAS, the City entered into an agreement previously with Larsen Larsen Nash & Larsen
(“Larsen law firm”)(“Agreement”) to provide indigent defense services for defendants
charged with certain violations of law in Bluffdale City;
WHEREAS, the City has determined that the Agreement attached to this resolution as Exhibit
A hereto is acceptable to the City and the Larsen Law firm and the Agreement complies with
the requirements of the law and is in the best interests of the City;

defense services to the Larsen law firm.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED BY THE BLUFFDALE CITY COUNCIL:

       SECTION 1. Authorization to Execute Agreement. The City Council hereby authorizes
the City Manager to execute an agreement between the City and the Larsen law firm for

      SECTION 2. Effective Date. This Resolution shall become effective immediately upon
passage and the City Council directs and authorizes the City Manager to execute any further
agreements related hereto.

                                     INDIGENT DEFENSE
                                   SERVICES AGREEMENT

        This Agreement is entered into this _____ day of ____________________, 2024 by and
between L. Bruse Larsen, of Larsen, Larsen, Nash & Larsen, Attorneys at Law, a professional
corporation located at 2974 West 3500 South, West Valley City, Utah, 84119 (hereinafter,
“Attorney”) and Bluffdale City, a municipal corporation of the State of Utah, having its principal
offices at 2222 West 14400 South, Bluffdale, Utah 84065 (hereinafter, the “City”).

                                         WITNESSETH

        WHEREAS, pursuant to Utah Code Ann. 77-32-101, et seq. (1953 as amended), City is
obligated to provide indigent defense counsel to persons who are charged with offenses alleging
violation of laws where there is a potential for incarceration prosecuted by City and to provide
that cow1sel that qualifies with the requirements of the 6th Amendment to the United States
Constitution; and

        WHEREAS, the City may fulfill this statutory duty through the appointment by contract
of qualified legal counsel who may provide indigent legal services; and

       WHEREAS, the provision of adequate indigent defense counsel is of paramount concern
and requires that the City contract with a provider that is able to provide qualified attorneys with
knowledge, experience, resources, preparation time and commitment to provide such services to
each individual indigent client; and

       WHEREAS, pursuant to the City Procurement Code, the City has awarded this
Agreement on the basis of demonstrated competence and qualification and at a fair and
reasonable price to a provider who is providing a professional service; and

        WHEREAS, City and Attorney have agreed upon a price for such services for the term
of this Agreement, which represents an amount sufficient to provide for the adequate defense
services and additionally to provide for any additional study, investigation or expertise that is
necessary to meet its legal requirement of providing defense counsel and Attorney feels will
compensate him sufficiently to handle all indigent defense work in an efficient and effective
manner that is in compliance with appropriate requirements of the 6th Amendment and all other
applicable rules and regulations; and

         WHEREAS, The City is engaging the Attorney to provide indigent defense services that
are completely independent of the City and the City recognizes that Attorney must be free to
defend the client zealously and without fear of termination, reduction in compensation, reduction
in staff or reduction in defense resources and that this Agreement provides for and ensures such
representation; and

        WHEREAS, The City recognizes the essential nature of the representation without any
conflicts of interest and the Attorney covenants herein to provide for such representation in
compliance with all rules of professional conduct; and


                                            Page 1 of 6
        WHEREAS, The City recognizes the need for adequate representation at all critical
stages of the criminal justice process and for any defendant where incarceration is possible and
guarantees this level of representation in this Agreement; and

        WHEREAS, The City recognizes that adequate representation includes representation
that tests the City’s evidence in a meaningful adversarial way including, Attorney’s ability, legal
training and experience to handle a case, Attorney’s access to adequate defense resources,
Attorney’s workload permits effective representation and reasonable continuity throughout a
case; and

       WHEREAS, the City further recognizes that representation must be given by Attorney
who is fairly compensated and that this Agreement provides for fair compensation; and

        WHEREAS, this Agreement specifically avoids improper incentives that would impair
the effective representation by the Attorney.

       NOW, THERFORE, the Parties agree as follows:

1. Attorney Qualifications.

       a. Attorneys certify that he and all members of his firm are members of the Utah State
          Bar and are in good standing. Attorney further certifies that he and all members of his
          firm are competent in the practice of criminal law and shall remain in good standing
          for the term of this Agreement.

       b. Attorney agrees to abide by all federal, state and local laws and to abide by the
          Cannon of Ethics and Rules of Professional Responsibility and Rules of Civility of
          the Utah State Bar.

       c. Attorney certifies that he is not currently, nor shall be, a party to any litigation which
          would place his licensing or standing with the Bar in jeopardy.

2. Attorney Requirements.

       a. Attorney shall provide quality representation and diligent advocacy to clients at all
          stages of representation and to all indigent defense cases assigned by the judge in the
          Bluffdale City Justice Court from July 1, 2024 through June 30, 2029.

       b. Attorney shall provide the services required under this Agreement according to the
          principles of a constitutionally adequate system including but not limited to the
          requirements as follows:

               i. Attorney agrees to preserve, protect and promote the Client’s rights as well as
                  the best interests of the client while maintaining loyalty to the client and
                  rendering effective assistance of counsel.



                                            Page 2 of 6
              ii. Attorney agrees to be available and accessible to clients reasonably in advance
                  of any hearing or trial.

              iii. Attorney is responsible to always appear for his assigned indigent defense
                   clients whenever and wherever Court is held on their cases.

              iv. Attorney is responsible to maintain adequate and proper records for the
                  representation for each assigned indigent defendant.

               v. Attorney agrees to be proficient in the applicable law.

              vi. Attorney agrees to acquire and maintain appropriate experience, skills and
                  training to match the complexity of the case.

             vii. Attorney agrees to devote adequate time and resources to each case and to
                  engage in proper preparation and adequate investigation.

            viii. Attorney shall endeavor to establish and maintain a relationship of trust and
                  open communication with the client and to keep the client informed as to the
                  status and progress of their case.

3. Reporting. Attorney shall be responsible to submit monthly billings to the City identifying
   cases assigned for representation under this Agreement.

4. Insurance. Attorney shall carry malpractice insurance in an amount and type approved by the
   City.

5. Payments. City shall pay Attorney for indigent defense services for the time period
   enumerated above in monthly installments in an amount equal to $200 per case assigned; an
   additional $50 per case removed to the District Court; an additional $150 for each bench trial
   handled during the billing period; an additional $300 for each jury trial handled during the
   billing period; and an additional $50 for each post-conviction hearing attended during the
   billing period beginning July 1, 2024 through the remainder of the contract.

6. Conflict of Interest Procedure. When Attorney determines that a conflict of interest exists
   that would cause Attorney’s representation of an indigent defendant to violate the Rules of
   Professional Conduct or prejudice said defendant’s right to competent representation,
   Attorney shall promptly arrange for conflict counsel. The City shall upon execution of this
   Agreement provide Attorney with $2,000.00 to be placed into Attorney’s trust account for
   the purpose of paying for conflict counsel as Attorney deems necessary. The Attorney shall
   provide the City with an annual report of such expenditures and the City shall annually bring
   the account balance to $2,000.00. In the event conflict counsel costs exceed $2,000 the City
   shall replenish the fund at its discretion after assessing the conflict issue.

7. Independent Experts and Investigation. The City shall provide to the Attorney a reserve fund
   of $2,000 to be placed in the Attorney’s trust account per City fiscal year to pay costs


                                           Page 3 of 6
   associated with service of process, witness fees, expert witnesses, investigators and other
   services required by Attorney to offer a competent representation for indigent defendants.
   These funds shall be for all costs of service of process and witness fees for witnesses required
   to be subpoenaed on behalf of the indigents who are represented under this Agreement. If
   Attorney believes these funds are insufficient to provide indigent defendants with competent
   representation, Attorney shall notify the City in writing of the shortfall, provide a detailed
   accounting of costs incurred and expected to be incurred, and provide an estimate of
   additional funds required. The City shall then consider Attorney’s request and determine
   whether the appropriation or allocation of additional funds is necessary and appropriate.

8. Appeals. In recognition of the additional cost of pursuing an appeal from the Bluffdale
   Justice Court to the District Court of the State of Utah the City shall compensate Attorney an
   additional $200 per case to handle said appeal in the District Court. All appeals to the Utah
   Court of Appeals or the Utah Supreme Court shall be the responsibility of the City via
   independent counsel.

9. Termination. This contract shall be terminable by either party upon thirty (30) days written
   notice.

10. Miscellaneous Provisions.

       a. Subcontract Assignment. The Attorney shall not assign any rights or interest herein
          without prior written consent of the City.

       b. Third Parties. Nothing in this Agreement shall create a contractual relationship with,
          or a cause of action in favor of, a third party against the City.

       c. Attorney’s Fees. In the event of default hereunder, the defaulting party agrees to pay
          all costs incurred by the non-defaulting party in enforcing this Agreement, including
          reasonable attorney’s fees, whether work is performed by in-house or outside counsel
          and whether incurred through initiation of legal proceedings or otherwise.

       d. Severability. In the event any provision of this Agreement is held to be invalid or
          unenforceable, the remaining provisions shall remain valid and binding upon the
          Parties.

11. Entire Agreement. This Agreement contains the entire and integrated agreement between the
    Parties, and no statement, promise, or inducements made by either Party or agents for either
    Party, which are not contained in this written Agreement, shall be binding or valid.

12. Modification of Agreement. This Agreement may be modified only by written amendment
    executed by all of the Parties hereto.

13. Applicable Law. This Agreement shall be governed by the laws of the State of Utah. Venue
    shall be in the State of Utah.



                                           Page 4 of 6
14. Binding on Successors. This Agreement shall bind and inure to the benefit of the Parties’
    partners, assigns, legal representatives, and successors in interest.

15. Captions and Headings. The section headings or captions appearing in this Agreement are for
    convenience only, are not a part of this Agreement, and are not to be considered in
    interpreting this Agreement.

16. Non-Waiver. No failure by any party to insist upon the strict performance of any covenant,
    duty, agreement or condition of this Agreement or to exercise any right or remedy
    consequent upon a breach thereof shall constitute a waiver of any such breach or of such or
    any other covenant, agreement, term or condition. Any party may, by written notice delivered
    in the manner provided in this Agreement, but shall be under no obligation to, waive any of
    its rights or any conditions to its obligations hereunder, or any duty, obligation or covenant of
    any other party. No waiver shall affect or alter the remainder of this Agreement but each and
    every other covenant, agreement, term and condition hereof shall continue in full force and
    effect with respect to any other then existing or subsequently occurring breach.

IN WITNESS WHEREOF, the Parties to this Agreement have executed this Agreement as of the
day and year first above written.

FY 2024-2025
BUDGET
This document is the Fiscal Year 2024-2025 budget for the City of Bluﬀdale. The budget is the
foundation for all the programs, services, and projects the City accomplishes each year.
Because of its importance to our City operations, a significant amount of time and eﬀort go
into its preparation. Personnel from all our departments provide input and expertise to
identify the needs and costs associated with their assigned areas.

Our methods of calculating and projecting our budget numbers improve each year, but the
underlying foundational approach continues to be the same. We focus on conservative fiscal
responsibility and a desire, at a minimum, to maintain our current service levels. For this
year’s budget we are in need of an increased service level in both Fire/Medical and Police. We
strive to address current needs and prepare for future needs in a way that is financially
sustainable in the future.

We are a service organization. Employees are our greatest asset. To this end, retaining,
training and attracting quality employees is one of our budget priorities. This year’s fiscal
budget maintains our exceptional service levels by providing the resources to allow the City to
retain well-trained and skilled employees. It addresses the need to build and maintain our
valuable public infrastructure. It also ensures financial stability by maintaining appropriate,
healthy financial reserves.

The Mayor and City Council have provided direction for their plans for the future, and this
budget provides the financial support to implement their plans. Their plans include key
initiatives expressed by and supported by the residents. These key initiatives improve our
lives and help create a thriving, caring community.

As our City continues to grow we have a responsibility to ensure that our investment in our
personnel and infrastructure has not been wasted. To support this responsibility, this budget
includes hiring 7 new employees: 2 additional patrol police oﬀicers and 5 additional full-time
equivalent employees in the public works departments. Additionally, the budget includes
upgrading two of the seven frontline positions in the fire department from part-time to full-
time.

Growth creates a demand for new and expanded infrastructure. Growth also impacts the
replacement cycle of equipment and aging infrastructure. This budget includes $8 million in
new and ongoing projects paid with City money. The budget also includes an additional $35
million of new and ongoing projects that are paid with money allocated from the state, grants
from state and county sources, and projects shared with other governmental entities.

All of these expenditures are designed to maintain and improve the quality of our lives. That
quality of life is further enhanced when our residents have opportunities to spend time with
one another. This budget includes several hundreds of thousands of dollars for recreation




                                               2
and sports programs, Old West Days activities, Bluﬀdale Arts events, Miss Bluﬀdale
Scholarship program, Healthy Bluﬀdale promotions, and various other City events.

This initial budget is a tentative budget and will change during the next several weeks. Please
join the City Council as they discuss and debate their current and future plans and priorities
that drive the budget each year.

Mark Reid
City Manager

We are presenting the proposed Budget for Bluffdale City (the "City" or "Bluffdale") for the July 2024 to June 2025 Fiscal Year (FY2025). The City has been a
fast growing city at the heart of Utah's largest two metropolitan areas. The rapid growth and location present challenges and opportunities that create
differing views within the City. This budget is an attempt to represent the needs and intent of the City Council and City residents.

The information contained herein is a summary of a more detailed report prepared by City Staff. This document is intended to help City residents better
understand the historical context of City operations, staffing, and finances. Charts detail the number of full-time equivalent employees ("FTE"s) in various
departments as well as historical revenues and expenditures. Additional information is available upon request. This is your City! Feel free to reach out to
members of the City Council, City Staff, or the Budget Review Committee (a committee of citizens who volunteer their time to help review and make sure
the budget is understandable). All of these people work to make sure you feel like this is YOUR City!

Actual property taxes are currently overstated for FY 2024. The County informed the City of an overdistribution of property taxes in November and
December, so current collections are ahead of typical actual amounts. Future distributions will be reduced until the overage has been recovered. We
estimate that it will take 4-5 months to make up the overdistribution. Our FY2024 projection has been adjusted to reflect expected revenue for the year.
Property taxes are expected to be largely flat compared with FY2023. The sales tax revenue growth rate in FY2024 is lower than the last few years. Sales
taxes for FY2025 are expected to be slightly higher than the current year. Increases in franchise tax revenue are expected to drive growth in the "Other
Taxes" category. The reduction in grants is primarily due to the elimination of COVID related federal grants. Also, fire department grants are reported in
the Fire and Police Protection Fund. Other revenues for FY2025 are expected to be similar to FY2024.

Impact fees are collected when developers build new businesses and homes. These fees are intended to offset the impacts of those new developments on the City's
infrastructure. Impact fees can generally only be used for the incremental infrastructure necessary to service the new businesses and homes from which they are collected.
Impact fees can only be collected after studies have identified specific projects for which those fees can be used.
